displayQuote: What I hear, I forget. What I say, I remember. What I do, I understand

meta.title: Who really said "What I hear, I forget. What I say, I remember. What I do, I understand"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lao Tzu. This proverb appears in no Laozi or Confucius text; its real ancestor is the philosopher Xunzi. The tidy modern wording is a paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What I hear, I forget. What I say, I remember. What I do, I understand'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lao Tzu. Wikiquote files this exact wording under 'Misattributed'; the genuine root is the Confucian philosopher Xunzi, ch. 8. The compact form is modern.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — a modern proverb rooted in Xunzi
answer.authorDates: c. 310 – c. 235 BCE · Chinese Confucian philosopher of the Warring States period
answer.sourceLine: The compact saying is pinned on Lao Tzu across quote sites and self-help books, but it appears in no Laozi text — Wikiquote files this exact wording under “Misattributed” on the Laozi page ↗. Its genuine ancestor is a line from the 3rd-century-BCE Confucian philosopher Xunzi; the tidy three-part English form is a modern paraphrase, not a literal translation of him or anyone else.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Xunzi 荀子, ch. 8 ‘Ru Xiao’ (The Achievements of the Ru)
Lao Tzu (also Confucius and Benjamin Franklin)

source.excerpt: “Not having heard of it is not as good as having heard of it. Having heard of it is not as good as having seen it. Having seen it is not as good as knowing it. Knowing it is not as good as putting it into practice. Learning arrives at putting it into practice and then stops.”
trail: Wikiquote files this exact wording under “Misattributed” on its Laozi page ↗, adding that it has also been wrongly pinned on Confucius.
The genuine ancestor is a line from Xunzi, ch. 8 ‘Ru Xiao’ ↗: hearing is worse than seeing, seeing worse than knowing, and knowing worse than putting into practice.

Quote Investigator ↗ traces the whole hear/see/do family to Xunzi (in English by Homer Dubs’s 1928 translation), with the tidy compact form surfacing only in the 20th century and later mis-credited to Benjamin Franklin.
No line resembling this appears in the Tao Te Ching; the attribution to Lao Tzu rests on quote sites and self-help books, none citing a Laozi source.
source.excerptNote: This is the authentic ancestor — Xunzi, ch. 8, in Eric L. Hutton’s translation. The popular “What I hear, I forget” line is a loose modern compression of this hearing/seeing/doing hierarchy, not a quotation of Lao Tzu.

source.rightsNote: The exact compact English wording is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase whose first publication is undocumented, so no public-domain status can be asserted for it. The ancient Xunzi text is long in the public domain, and Homer Dubs’s 1928 English translation is also US public domain — but neither is the wording popularized under Lao Tzu’s name.

author.name: Xun Kuang (Xunzi)
author.heading: About Xunzi
author.metaLine: c. 310 – c. 235 BCE · Chinese Confucian philosopher of the Warring States period
author.bio: Xun Kuang, known as Xunzi, was a leading Confucian thinker of the late Warring States period. Working in the generation after Mencius, he argued that human nature must be shaped through learning, ritual, and above all practice. His chapter on the Ru ranks mere hearing below seeing, and seeing below doing — the seed of the modern “I hear, I forget” proverb that is wrongly hung on Lao Tzu.

cite.sourceCitation: Xunzi, “The Achievements of the Ru” (Ru Xiao), ch. 8, in Xunzi: The Complete Text, trans. Eric L. Hutton (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2014). Popular “What I hear, I forget…” wording: anonymous modern English paraphrase, first publication undocumented.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘What I hear, I forget. What I say, I remember. What I do, I understand’?” Last verified 10 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: Popularly attributed to Lao Tzu, but misattributed — it appears in no Laozi or Confucius text. The idea descends from the 3rd-century-BCE Confucian philosopher Xunzi (ch. 8, "The Achievements of the Ru"); the compact "What I hear / say / do" wording is a modern English paraphrase of unknown authorship.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: This tidy aphorism is a magnet for big philosopher names. It is stamped on Lao Tzu across quote sites and self-help books, and just as often on Confucius — but it is in the surviving work of neither.

items.why: No line resembling this appears in the Tao Te Ching or any Laozi text; Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” ↗ on the Laozi page.
Constantly captioned “Confucius” on image quotes, yet it is absent from the Analects; the same Wikiquote entry ↗ flags the Confucius credit as an error too.
A cousin form — “Tell me and I forget, teach me and I remember, involve me and I learn” — is often stamped on Franklin, but Quote Investigator finds no evidence ↗ he wrote it.

misattribution.truthLine: The real ancestor is the 3rd-century-BCE Confucian philosopher Xunzi ↗, whose chapter 8 ranks hearing below seeing, seeing below knowing, and knowing below doing — the compact “What I hear / say / do” version is a modern English paraphrase, not his exact words.

context.heading: Why the line travels so well
lead: The saying is really a slogan for experiential learning — the idea that we retain little of what we passively hear, more of what we witness, and most of what we do ourselves. That message is genuinely old: it is the backbone of Xunzi’s argument that a scholar’s knowledge is proven only when it is put into practice.

What changed is the packaging. In the 20th century the hierarchy was compressed into a rhythmic three-beat couplet and, as it spread through classrooms and management training, acquired ever more prestigious — and ever more wrong — bylines: Confucius, Lao Tzu, even Benjamin Franklin.
context.pull: We remember what we do — but not who first said so.
